title: Stress, today
what: A day view with a one line verdict, hours split into Rest, Low, Medium and High, and a 24 hour bar timeline coloured blue for rest and orange for stress.
takeaway: Lead with one plain sentence about the day before any chart, and show stress as time spent in bands rather than a single number.

title: Stress Monitor
what: A 0 to 3 gauge reading 1.2 Medium at a set time, a line chart across the day, a bar comparing today to a typical Monday, and a coach note that stress peaked at 8:09am after a short night.
takeaway: Compare the user to their own typical day and tie a peak to a likely cause such as short sleep.

title: Stress Rhythm Score
what: A score of 78 with a bar for each recent day, a stress timeline with a threshold line and activity icons, and a closing line saying the user was relaxed for 63% of the day.
takeaway: A daily score with a short week of bars above the detail gives quick day to day context.

title: Daytime Stress
what: A chart with four named zones (Stressed, Engaged, Relaxed, Restored), toggles for movement and tags, an Add a tag button, totals for Stressed and Restored time, and a daily summary that opens with praise.
takeaway: Let users add tags on the stress chart so the reading and its cause live in one place, and name zones in friendly words.

title: Stress management score, no data
what: The stress score page shows No score because the device was not worn long enough, but still shows a manual mood entry of Stressed at 12:13 AM.
takeaway: For users with no wearable, a self reported entry can fill the stress page instead of leaving it empty.

title: Log mood
what: A single question with five chips from Very calm to Very stressed, with Stressed selected, plus date and time fields.
takeaway: Five labelled chips on a calm to stressed scale is a fast check-in that older users can read without a slider.

title: State of Mind
what: Asks how you have felt overall today, with a slider from Very Unpleasant to Very Pleasant, a shape that changes with the value and a word label (Slightly Pleasant).
takeaway: A slider that always shows a plain word for the current value avoids asking users to judge numbers.

title: Exertion check-in
what: One screen asks how much you exerted yourself today, with 0 to 3 buttons for Physically, Mentally, Emotionally and Socially, and a toggle to reuse previous answers.
takeaway: A small grid with big tap targets and a reuse yesterday toggle makes a daily load check-in very quick.

title: I often feel stressed or anxious
what: A statement with an illustration of a tense person and a 0 to 10 slider set near 6.
takeaway: Framing the question as a statement to agree with feels softer than asking for a stress rating.

title: Choose Event Type
what: A sheet to add a timeline event, with Stress offered as a type next to Workout, Breathwork, Food, Activity and Other.
takeaway: Logging a stressful moment can sit in the same add menu as meals and workouts, which GoodFlip users already know.

title: Identify negative stories
what: An intro to a reframing exercise showing example beliefs (I am not enough, I am always struggling) written on paper being burned by a match.
takeaway: Show sample thoughts before asking users to write their own, so they know what kind of thought to name.

title: Give unfounded worries a reality check
what: Step 1 of 6 of a worry exercise asks whether most worries stay just worries, with an optional note field and a Save to new moment link.
takeaway: Short numbered cards with one question each, and an optional note, keep a CBT tool light enough to finish daily.

title: Home with SOS
what: The home screen has a red outlined SOS pill fixed in the top bar above self-care shortcuts and a chat card.
takeaway: An always visible SOS entry in the header means help is one tap away from anywhere.

title: Are you in crisis?
what: The SOS page lists two local helplines, then offers Create Safety Plan and Grounding for panic for users who cannot make a call.
takeaway: Separate the crisis path (helplines) from the calm-down path (grounding) on one page so the user picks what fits.

title: Reframing strategies
what: A grid of reframing exercises with line drawings and names like Bright Spots, Lens Shift, Self Talk and Time Travel.
takeaway: Give each CBT tool a friendly name and a simple drawing so a weekly assigned tool feels like a thing, not a worksheet.

title: Bright Spots intro
what: A full card with the exercise name, a one line purpose and a single Begin button.
takeaway: One sentence of purpose and one button is enough before starting.

title: Step 1
what: Step 1 asks the user to breathe deeply through the nose, with a drawing, audio control and a dotted progress bar.
takeaway: Open a reframe with a breath so the user is calm before thinking about the thought, and offer audio for those who prefer listening.

title: Step 6
what: The last step asks the user to find a good or neutral feeling inside and thank themselves for it.
takeaway: End on a small positive action rather than a summary, so the tool closes warmly.

title: How helpful was it?
what: A closing card asks how helpful the exercise was, with three round buttons: Not helpful, A little helpful, Very helpful.
takeaway: A three choice helpfulness rating after a tool gives the coach a signal of what works for each person.

title: My progress, stress
what: An empty monthly chart with Stress and Anxiety tabs, a note to start tracking stress with monthly check-ins, and a Check in button.
takeaway: Explain the rhythm of the check-in (monthly) right on the empty chart.

title: Check-in question
what: Question 1 of 10 asks how often in the last month you were upset by something unexpected, with five options from Very often to Never.
takeaway: Plain frequency words as large tappable rows make a validated scale feel like a simple chat.

title: Last question
what: Question 10 of 10 about difficulties piling up, with Sometimes selected and a counter at the top.
takeaway: Show a clear count so the user knows how close they are to done.

title: Results
what: A score of 23 labelled Moderate stress on a three part bar (Low 0 to 13, Moderate 14 to 26, High 27 to 40), a kind framing line and suggested content.
takeaway: Pair the score with its band and range, a non judging sentence, and a next thing to do.

title: Stress Monitor sessions
what: Below a summary of time in high stress, the monitor offers two guided breathing sessions, Increase Relaxation and Increase Alertness.
takeaway: Put the calm-down action directly under the stress reading so a high moment leads straight to a pause.

title: Session details
what: A detail page explaining the breathing exercise, its breathing rate and a 3 minute duration, with a Start Exercise button.
takeaway: State the length up front so users know the pause is short.

title: Inhale
what: An orange ring grows with the cue Inhale through the nose and a countdown at the top.
takeaway: A growing ring plus one short instruction is all the screen needs during breathing.

title: Exhale
what: The ring turns blue and widens with the cue Exhale slowly through the mouth and empty your lungs.
takeaway: Change colour between in and out breaths so the phase is clear without reading.

title: Saved
what: A green check in a circle with the word Saved.
takeaway: A quiet confirmation that the session counted is enough to close a pause.

title: How are you today?
what: A bottom sheet labelled 1st daily check in with five faces from Awful to Great.
takeaway: Start the trigger log with one tap on how you are, before asking why.

title: What is having the biggest impact?
what: Feeling words, then a grid of life areas such as Health, Family, Work, Tasks and Partner under the question what is having the biggest impact.
takeaway: A grid of everyday causes turns identifying a stress trigger into a tap, no typing needed.

title: Tags selected
what: Calm and Peaceful plus Health and Spirituality are filled yellow, with Complete Check in and Start Journal Entry buttons.
takeaway: Offer a finish now button and an optional write more button so the short version always counts.

title: Saved entry
what: The journal entry shows the chosen face and tags as small chips above the written note.
takeaway: Keep the picked trigger tags attached to the entry so patterns can be shown back later.
